analysis.one_liner: Lets banks, securities firms, and insurance companies combine into single financial conglomerates, repealing the Glass-Steagall wall between them.
analysis.headline: Congress repealed the Glass-Steagall separation of banking, securities, and insurance; the final votes were 90-8 in the Senate and 362-57 in the House, and the President signed it into law on November 12, 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: For most of the 20th century, federal law barred banks from merging with Wall Street securities firms and insurance companies. This law tore down those walls: a 'financial holding company' could now own a bank, a brokerage, and an insurer under one roof, and it preempted some state rules that stood in the way. It also added a financial-privacy title requiring banks to tell customers when personal data would be shared with outside companies and to let customers opt out, an ATM fee-disclosure rule, and some Community Reinvestment Act conditions.
analysis.who_benefits: Large, well-capitalized financial companies gain the right to merge banking, securities underwriting, and insurance under one holding company and to offer one-stop financial shopping. Securities firms gain access to bank deposits and bank customers; insurers gain the ability to affiliate with banks; the biggest institutions gain freedom from Depression-era affiliation bans [S5][S6].

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Glass-Steagall Act provisions that barred a bank from affiliating with a securities firm and barred interlocking directors between banks and securities firms [S2][S5][S6].

Creates 'financial holding companies' that may engage in any activity the Federal Reserve determines to be financial in nature — lending, insurance, securities underwriting, investment advisory, and merchant banking — provided every insured depository subsidiary is well capitalized and well managed [S5][S6].

Conditions the new powers on Community Reinvestment Act compliance: a financial holding company cannot commence new activities or acquire companies if any insured depository subsidiary has less than a 'satisfactory' CRA rating [S5][S6].

Requires ATM operators to disclose fees at the time of service and requires financial institutions to give customers notice and an opportunity to opt out before sharing nonpublic personal information with nonaffiliated third parties, and criminalizes obtaining customer financial information by false pretenses ('pretexting') [S4][S5].

Keeps state functional regulation of insurance and McCarran-Ferguson in place, requires physical segregation of banking and insurance sales, and bars banks from conditioning credit on buying the bank's own insurance products [S4][S5].

analysis.who_pays: Bank customers, who must affirmatively opt out — or lose protection entirely for data shared among a company's own affiliates — of having their personal financial information shared; states, which lose some authority to regulate bank-insurance combinations; and smaller banks and independent insurance agents, who face competition from newly merged giants [S4][S5].

drawbacks.text: The privacy title gives consumers only the right to 'opt out' of sharing data with nonaffiliated third parties; sharing customer information among a holding company's own affiliates is permitted by default, and an opt-out does not stop it [S4][S5].

The law preempts state laws that restrict affiliations between banks and insurers and bars states from regulating the insurance activities of banks in ways that disadvantage them, narrowing state consumer protections [S2][S5].

For institutions whose failure could destabilize the financial system, the bill orders only a study of whether they should hold subordinated debt — no new requirement — while lifting several Federal Reserve safety restrictions, including the stock-loan limit and some examination authority over functionally regulated affiliates [S5][S6].

Small banks with 'satisfactory' records get less frequent CRA examinations, and small rural banks under $100 million in assets are exempted from CRA in the Senate version — reducing the enforcement of lending obligations to low- and moderate-income communities [S3][S5].

The House voted 241-132 to instruct its conferees to secure 'the strongest consumer financial privacy protections possible,' including an opt-in right to say no to marketing uses of data, but the final law's Title V provides only notice and opt-out [S10][S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The case for the bill was that Depression-era walls between banking, securities, and insurance were obsolete, and that American firms were losing to foreign conglomerates; customers were promised one-stop shopping and more competition. The bill did carry real consumer items — ATM fee disclosure, a pretexting ban, anti-tying rules, CRA conditions on the new powers. But its center of gravity is unmistakably the industry's agenda: the privacy protections are opt-out rather than the opt-in standard privacy advocates sought, several state-level protections are preempted, and the safety question that mattered most — what happens when institutions become 'too big to fail' — was answered with a study rather than a requirement. The bill is well designed for the firms it liberates; the protections for customers were the concessions, not the core.

outcome.mechanism: It moved fast: the Senate passed it 54-44 in May 1999, the House replaced the Senate text with its own version and passed it without objection in July, a conference committee blended the two over five meetings, and both chambers approved the conference report in early November by landslide margins before the President signed it.

narrative.text: The Senate Banking Committee held hearings in February 1999, ordered an original measure reported, and Senator Gramm reported it to the floor on April 28, 1999 [S8].
The Senate passed the bill 54-44 on May 6, 1999: 53 of 55 Republicans voted yes and 44 of 45 Democrats voted no [S9].
On July 20, 1999 the House, at Chairman Leach's request, struck the Senate text and inserted the provisions of its own financial modernization bill (H.R. 10), passing it without objection [S8].

Before the conference, the House voted 241-132 to instruct conferees to seek the strongest possible consumer financial and medical privacy protections, with Democrats supporting the instruction 182-1 and Republicans opposing it 131-58 [S10].
Conferees met five times between September 23 and October 28, 1999, then agreed to file the conference report, which was filed November 2 [S8].
The Senate agreed to the conference report 90-8 (Republicans 52-1, Democrats 38-7) on November 4, and the House agreed 362-57 (Republicans 207-5, Democrats 155-51) the same day [S11][S12].
The President signed it on November 12, 1999, and it became Public Law 106-102 [S8][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest banks, securities firms, and insurance companies, which could now consolidate into financial conglomerates; the well-capitalized institutions that moved first gained the most from the new financial holding company structure.

sides.party_line_note: Senate passage split sharply by party — Republicans 53-0 in favor, Democrats 44-1 against — but the final conference report drew heavy bipartisan support (Senate 90-8, House 362-57 with 155 Democrats in favor) after privacy and Community Reinvestment Act provisions were added.

industries.industry: Large banks and bank holding companies
industries.note: Banks won the right to merge with securities firms and insurers under one financial holding company, ending the Glass-Steagall separation, though the new powers are conditioned on satisfactory Community Reinvestment Act ratings and well-capitalized subsidiaries. For customers this meant one-stop shopping and more competition, but also default data-sharing among a conglomerate's own affiliates.

Securities firms gained access to bank deposits and bank branch networks, and banks gained the ability to underwrite securities — enabling conglomerates like Citigroup's structure. Securities activities stay under SEC functional regulation, and Federal Reserve examination authority over these subsidiaries is narrowed.

Insurers gained the right to affiliate with or acquire banks, but national banks are barred from underwriting most insurance as principal, state functional regulation and McCarran-Ferguson are preserved, and some state affiliation laws are preempted. Independent insurance agents lose their protected position against bank competition.

Banks can now sell insurance across state lines under Barnett Bank preemption standards, and the bill preempts state rules that single banks out; small agents face competition from bank-owned distribution. The bill does preserve state licensing and some sales-practice rules.

industries.industry: Financial institutions as holders of customer data
industries.note: The law makes sharing customers' nonpublic personal information among a company's own affiliates the legal default: customers must opt out to stop sharing with nonaffiliated third parties, and an opt-out does not reach affiliate sharing at all. This locks in the conglomerates' ability to market using customer data gathered at the bank.

Community banks gained regulatory relief — less frequent CRA exams, easier Federal Home Loan Bank advances, S corporation expansion — but also faced competition from newly formed giants, and the Comptroller General was directed to study the act's impact on banks with $100 million or less in assets.
